Purpose Physique athletes engage in rigorous competition preparation involving intense energy restriction and physical training to enhance muscle definition. This study investigates hormonal changes and their physiological and performance impacts during such preparation. Methods Participants included female (10 competing (COMP) and 10 non-dieting controls (CTRL)) and male (13 COMP and 10 CTRL) physique athletes. COMP participants were tested 23 weeks before (PRE), one week before (MID), and 23 weeks after the competition (POST). Non-dieting CTRL participants were tested at similar intervals. Measurements included body composition (DXA), muscle cross-sectional area (ultrasound), energy availability (EA) derived by subtracting exercise energy expenditure (EEE) from energy intake (EI) and dividing by fat-free mass (FFM), muscle strength, and various serum hormone concentrations (ACTH, cortisol, estradiol, FSH, IGF-1, IGFBP-3, insulin, and free and total testosterone and SHBG). Results During the diet, EA ( p < 0.001), IGF-1 ( p < 0.001), IGFBP-3 ( p < 0.01), and absolute muscle strength ( p < 0.01–0.001) decreased significantly in both sexes in COMP. Decreases in IGF-1 were also associated with higher loss in FFM. In males, testosterone ( p < 0.01) and free testosterone ( p < 0.05) decreased, while SHBG ( p < 0.001) and cortisol ( p < 0.05) increased. Insulin decreased significantly only in males ( p < 0.001). Mood disturbances, particularly increased fatigue in males ( p < 0.05), highlighted the psychological strain of competition preparation. All these changes were restored by increased EA during the post-competition recovery period. Conclusion Significant reductions in IGF-1 and IGFBP-3 during competition preparation may serve as biomarkers for monitoring physiological stress. This study offers valuable insights into hormonal changes, muscle strength, and mood state during energy-restricted intense training. Keywords Energy availability IGF-1 Weight loss Bodybuilding POMS REDs Finnish Fitness Sports Association Renaissance Periodization University of Jyväskylä (JYU) Open Access funding provided by University of Jyväskylä (JYU). issue-copyright-statement © Springer-Verlag GmbH Germany, part of Springer Nature 2025 Introduction Physique athletes undergo rigorous competition preparation with intense energy restriction and physical training to enhance muscle definition. This preparatory phase is followed by a recovery period of 3–4 months, during which body composition and endocrine changes are typically restored (Hulmi et al. 2017 ; Rossow et al. 2013 ). The off-season focuses on muscle growth through balanced nutrition and resistance training (Mursu et al. 2023 ). Hormone profiles in elite athletes differ from usual reference ranges, potentially reflecting baseline differences between athletes and the general population as well as the impact of athletic training on the endocrine systems (Healy et al. 2014 ). We previously reported that physique athletes experience significant hormonal changes during the competition preparation. These inevitable changes, likely caused by the combined factors of weight loss, training and dieting stress, and the sustained energy deficit, include reduced leptin and T3 levels and increased ghrelin concentrations, reflecting shifts in energy metabolism (Isola et al. 2023 ). Weight loss also alters serum cardiometabolic profiles, such as insulin, highlighting metabolic complexities (Jouhki et al. 2024 ; Mäestu et al. 2010 ). Additionally, male athletes experience fluctuations in insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), free (FT), and total testosterone (T), while female athletes demonstrate changes in estradiol levels during the preparation (Hulmi et al. 2017 ; Mitchell et al. 2018 ). Athletes may also experience reductions in muscular function, strength, and power as the focus shifts toward achieving ideal body aesthetics sometimes at the expense of exercise performance (Robinson et al. 2015 ). Additionally, bone mineral density (BMD) can decrease during periods of energy deficit, but it often recovers during refeeding (Hulmi et al. 2017 ). The physiological stress from the competition preparation may lead to disruptions in sleep patterns, mood disturbances, and alterations in nutrient intake, which collectively contribute to diminished exercise performance (Longstrom et al. 2020 ). The concept of relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S) expands our understanding of low energy availability (LEA) impacts. Affecting both male and female athletes, RED-S leads to hormonal imbalances, decreased bone mineral density, and weakened immune function. Energy deficiency also reduces muscle strength, power, and endurance, and can cause mood disturbances, anxiety, and depression. These changes impair reproductive function, metabolism, and overall health, causing conditions like hypothalamic amenorrhea in females and reduced fertility in males. Ultimately, RED-S compromises health, well-being, and athletic performance (Angelidi et al. 2024 ). This study examined serum hormonal changes in physique athletes during the competition preparation. Understanding hormonal alterations vital to training and health outcomes is paramount, as it may inform coaching strategies. This research delves into how energy restriction and intense training impact hormone profiles, physiological performance, and psychological well-being, using the profile of mood states (POMS) to assess mood changes. We hypothesized that the competition diets would lead to changes in serum hormones, BMD, performance, and mood in both sexes. These findings may potentially improve coaching methods for supporting athletes while minimizing adverse effects from competition preparation.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Rigorous competition preparation in physique athletes, involving intense energy restriction and physical training, leading to a weight-loss period and a state of energy deficiency.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: Hormonal changes, muscle strength reduction, and mood shifts are primarily driven by intense energy restriction, physical training, and the resulting sustained energy deficit and low energy availability (LEA). Decreased IGF-1 is associated with higher fat-free mass (FFM) loss, and its reduction is crucial for muscle development and protein synthesis. Decreases in testosterone and free testosterone in males are linked to disruptions in the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal (HPG) axis. Increased SHBG results from significant weight loss due to reduced caloric intake, leading to less bioavailable free testosterone. The decreased Testosterone/Cortisol (T/C) ratio indicates heightened physiological stress and an imbalance between anabolic and catabolic processes, potentially exacerbated by psychological stress. These changes collectively reflect physiological stress, altered energy metabolism, and hormonal imbalances, with most adverse effects showing recovery upon increased energy availability post-competition. Adequate energy availability and structured nutrition are essential to maintaining hormonal balance, muscle mass, and performance.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: Hormonal, strength, and mood changes were observed during the 'diet' phase (PRE to MID, 23 weeks before to one week before competition), characterized by a 21-week weight loss period and significant decreases in Energy Availability (EA) in both sexes compared to controls. EA significantly decreased from 43.9  1 10.8 to 27.0  1 5.28 kcal/kg (males) and from 38.2  1 6.9 to 20.8  1 3.50 kcal/kg (females). These changes, including the decrease in the T/C ratio and increased fatigue, generally reversed or recovered during the post-competition recovery phase (MID to POST), when energy availability increased (p < 0.05), indicating a direct correlation between the intensity and duration of energy restriction and the observed changes. The timing of these changes and recoveries suggests a temporal dose-response to the competitive activity.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: Significant sex-specific differences were observed. Insulin decreased significantly only in males (p < 0.001), with only a non-significant trend in females. Testosterone, free testosterone, and cortisol changes were predominantly observed or more pronounced in males. Male COMP participants also experienced lower EA at MID compared to female COMP (p < 0.01), uniquely exhibited a loss in lean mass, and showed increased fatigue and tension. While IGF-1 and IGFBP-3 reductions, and decreases in absolute muscle strength (isometric force, concentric torque) were significant in both sexes, SHBG increased in both. Estradiol showed differential changes and a male-specific decrease post-competition. Strength training during preparation may protect bone mineral content and density, contrasting with findings in endurance athletes. Many changes were specific to competition preparation groups (COMP) when compared to non-dieting controls (CTRL).

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Female and male physique athletes undergoing rigorous competition preparation (including amateur athletes aiming for national championships), and healthy non-dieting control participants. Exclusion criteria included individuals with chronic diseases, medication affecting measured variables, junior or master competitors, and those not adhering to WADA guidelines.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: Competition preparation leads to significant physiological stress, hormonal imbalances (e.g., reduced anabolic hormones like IGF-1, testosterone, free testosterone; altered SHBG, estradiol, insulin, and increased cortisol in males), and mood disturbances (increased fatigue and tension in males, menstrual irregularities in females). These changes coincide with reduced physical performance (decreased muscle strength). IGF-1, IGFBP-3, and T/C ratio are identified as potential biomarkers for monitoring physiological stress and anabolic-catabolic balance. While these adverse changes can reflect aspects of Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (RED-S), a 21-week weight loss period did not, on average, negatively impact bone health (Z-scores remained stable), possibly due to strength training. Most adverse changes showed recovery post-competition with increased energy availability. Monitoring psychological well-being is crucial to mitigate adverse effects of low energy availability and prevent extreme symptoms of RED-S. Implementing structured and individualized nutrition plans focusing on energy and protein requirements, alongside mental health support, can minimize adverse effects and optimize performance.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: Adverse risk (due to physiological stress, hormonal imbalances, decreased muscle strength, psychological distress, and potential for RED-S), with diagnostic utility for biomarkers like IGF-1, IGFBP-3, and T/C ratio. Risk management strategies focus on mitigating these adverse effects, supporting mental well-being, and optimizing training/nutrition. There is also a protective benefit from implemented strategies and strength training for bone health.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: IGF-1 and IGFBP-3 are considered reliable, sex-neutral biomarkers for monitoring physiological stress during competition preparation. The Testosterone/Cortisol (T/C) ratio is a valuable marker for assessing anabolic-catabolic balance and optimizing training. Various blood assays (ACTH, Testosterone, Insulin, Cortisol, IGF-1, IGFBP-3, Estradiol, FSH, SHBG, Free Testosterone) showed acceptable sensitivity and intra-assay/inter-assay coefficients of variation (CVs), though some, like Testosterone and Estradiol, had higher CVs (16.3%/24.3% and 9.9%/16% respectively) which might affect precision. Limitations include the follow-up study design precluding reliable causality assessment, potential inaccuracies in estimating exercise energy expenditure (EEE) and overall energy availability (EA) in real-life, and not fully accounting for menstrual cycle variability or excluding hormonal contraceptive users in females, impacting female hormonal data interpretation. Fat-Free Mass (FFM) was found to mirror Lean Mass (LM) behavior, suggesting FFM is a reliable proxy for LM.
recommended_alternatives: Fat-Free Mass (FFM) as an alternative to Lean Mass (LM) for calculating Energy Availability (EA)
